headline_hi: मज़दूरों के बच्चों को मिला सहारा
summary_en: Every morning, children's smiles blossom at a construction site in Gurugram. Laborers working here leave their children at the Mobile Creches center. Lalita, a care worker at the center, waits for the children starting at eight in the morning. She takes complete care of every child's health and needs. Lalita has been doing this noble work with full dedication for the past twelve years. At the age of twenty, she chose this path after seeing a training center. She funded her education with her salary and also earned a B.Ed. degree. Now she runs the Ashiyana center and bridge courses for children. Because of this center, parents are able to go to work without any worry. The Mobile Creches organization has been transforming the lives of lakhs of children for the past fifty-seven years. Dedicated didis like Lalita are becoming a true inspiration for society.

lead.title: 1 Million Children, 57 Years: How Mobile Creches is Building a Childcare Infrastructure for Working Parents
lead.summary: This article has been published in partnership with Mobile Creches. By 8 am, the first children are walking into the creche at Aashiyana, a construction site in Gurugram where their parents work. Lalita is already there. "We look at every child from head to toe," she says. "Then we talk to the parents. What did the child eat last night? How did they sleep? Is anything troubling them?" It is a small ritual, repeated for 48 children every morning. For mothers who hand their children over and walk back into a day of work, it matters most. "A mother going to work may not know everything the child learns here," Lalita says. "What she knows is that one didi is taking care of her child and she can work in peace."   At a construction site in Gurugram, parents begin their workday while their children head to the Mobile Creches centre, where care worker Lalita is ready to welcome them.   Lalita, 32, has been that didi (elder sister/care giver) for nearly 12 years, a milestone she completes this November. As India marks the UN Global Day for Care and Support on 29 October, and Mobile Creches hosts its India Childcare Champions Awards a day earlier, her story asks a bigger question: what does it take to care for a country's youngest children well, and who should share the load? The teacher who stayed At 20, Lalita, then a private school teacher, noticed a Mobile Creches training centre near her home in South Delhi. "I felt strongly that yes, I should work here," she says. She now runs Aashiyana and its bridge course. summary_en: There is a village named Hiware Bazar in the Ahilyanagar district of Maharashtra. According to Sarpanch Popatrao Pawar, in the early nineties, nearly ninety percent of the village's people had migrated out. At that time, only thirteen percent of the land could be irrigated. This area falls in a low-rainfall region and receives around four hundred millimeters of rain annually. After this, Hiware Bazar utilized drought relief funds. Trenches were dug in the village and water conservation structures were built. This improved the agricultural land, and the families who had left returned. In the year 2015, when there was nearly fifty percent less rainfall than normal, crop production here still did not decline. This track record built through relief work continues to prove very useful today.

lead.title: As India's Weakest Monsoon in Over a Decade Hits Maharashtra, One Village Shows What Relief Work Can Build
lead.summary: According to its sarpanch, Popatrao Pawar, around 90% of the residents of Hiware Bazar, a village in Maharashtra's Ahilyanagar district (earlier Ahmednagar), had migrated by the early 1990s, and only 13% of its farmland could be irrigated.  The village lies in a rain shadow and receives about 400 mm of rain a year. Down To Earth reported in 2017 that its crop production did not fall in 2015, when it received around 50% less rain than normal. That record carries fresh relevance. India's monsoon ended 12.6% below average, its weakest in more than a decade, a senior India Meteorological Department official told Reuters on 30 September, 2026. Maharashtra recorded an 18% deficit and declared 265 of its 358 tehsils drought-affected on 26 September, 2026. A rulebook from 1880 Paying people to build public assets during drought is an old idea. The Famine Commission of 1880 recommended Famine Codes to guide officials in anticipating and relieving crop failure.  According to economist Jean Drèze, their backbone was public works paying subsistence wages within reach of workers' homes, supported by early warning, with specific guidelines on how to recognise and declare a famine.    Hiware Bazar used drought relief funds to build contour trenches and water-harvesting structures, restoring farmland and bringing migrant families home.   After Independence, the codes became Scarcity Manuals, and during the 1972-73 drought in Maharashtra, as many as 5 million people attended relief works at the peak of distress. Public works remain part of the response. headline_hi: ऑस्ट्रेलिया में सौर ऊर्जा का रिकॉर्ड
summary_en: Australia has created history in the field of renewable energy. On September 22, more than eighty percent of the country's electricity was generated from solar and wind. In the afternoon, rooftop solar panels on homes performed wonders. These rooftop panels fulfilled more than half of the total electricity demand on their own. In Australia, solar panels have now been installed in more than 4.3 million homes. The remaining electricity was supplied by large solar parks, wind turbines, and hydro power. During this period, the use of fuels like coal and gas was only twenty percent. Energy Minister Chris Bowen described this as a major victory for clean and affordable electricity. The surplus electricity was stored safely in large batteries and hydro storage. Experts say this record could be broken again in the coming weeks. This success shows how much ordinary people can change the earth together.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: Australia sets a new renewable energy record, with rooftop solar leading the way
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM On Saturday, September 22, solar and wind met 80.4 percent of demand on Australia’s national electricity market, with the grid covering the eastern states, South Australia, and the Australian Capital Territory. For about 30 minutes around lunchtime, rooftop panels on homes and businesses across the country carried more than half of the total load by themselves. Large-scale solar and wind farms covered most of the rest, with hydro adding around one percent. Fossil fuels accounted for 20 percent. Rooftop solar as a grid-scale contributor More than 4.3 million Australian households now have rooftop solar installed. Saturday’s record showed what those installations add up to in practice: enough distributed generation to carry the country through the middle of the day without needing much from the main grid at all. Energy Minister Chris Bowen called it “more clean, cheap, sovereign energy powering our homes and businesses than ever before,” and said more records should be expected as the transition continues. Why these records will keep falling Dr. Dylan McConnel l, an energy systems researcher at the University of New South Wales, called it “record season” for renewables. The conditions helped: clear sunny days, low demand from heating and cooling, and timing that landed right as a full year of new generation capacity came online all at once. “These records are probably not going to last very long,” McConnell said. “They’re probably going to be broken in the next couple of weeks.” Some of the surplus went into pumped hydro storage and batteries. headline_hi: बुजुर्ग महिला के लिए उमड़ा प्यार
headline_en: Outpouring of Love for an Elderly Woman
summary_en: Heartwarming news of humanity has emerged from the US state of Tennessee. An elderly woman worked at a movie theater in the city of Maryville. She was forced to work there even after passing the retirement age. A young man visiting the theater noticed her hard work and predicament. He launched an online fundraising campaign to help the elderly woman. People across the internet contributed enthusiastically to this drive. In no time, people raised one hundred and forty-six thousand dollars. Receiving such a large sum filled the elderly woman with joy and astonishment. Now she will be able to leave her job and live a peaceful retired life. This is not the first time young people have taken such a step for senior citizens. The generosity of strangers proved that goodness is still alive in the world.

headline_hi: अस्पतालों में मशीनों का शोर कम
summary_en: The Royal Cornwall Hospitals Trust in the UK has launched a unique initiative. In the year 2023, the trust started the 'Silent Hospital Pilot Project'. It is a three-year study. Its objective is to reduce alarm fatigue and noise in hospitals. Hospital ICUs experience a constant noise level of fifty to seventy decibels, which sometimes reaches up to one hundred decibels. According to the World Health Organization, a sound level of thirty decibels is suitable for rest. The investigation revealed that staff have to hear hundreds of alarms in every shift. In ninety percent of these cases, immediate medical attention is not required. In this project, instead of suppressing the sound, it is transmitted as data. The results of its second phase have been so encouraging that other UK hospitals are also preparing to adopt it.

lead.title: The Hospital That Silenced the Machines
lead.summary: B eep. Beep. Beep. The heartbeat monitor chirps. Hospitals have long tried to fight acoustic chaos with passive tactics — hanging sound-absorbing ceiling tiles, laying soft rubber flooring or begging clinical staff to whisper in the corridors. Beep. Beep. Beep. Blood pressure drops. But the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust in the United Kingdom has been trying something different. Instead of regarding noise as an inevitable physical nuisance that needs to be muffled, it treats sound as data that can be routed. In 2023, the trust launched the Silent Hospital Pilot Project , a three-year study exploring how to target “alarm fatigue” and noise pollution on hospital wards. As the second phase of the pilot comes to an end, its outcomes have already been so promising that other hospital networks around the U.K. are preparing to follow suit. Beep. Beep. Beep. Oxygen levels dip. Hospital wards are notoriously loud, with continuous background noise on intensive care units , for example, often averaging 50 to 70 decibels (dB), comparable to heavy traffic, and sharp peaks frequently passing 80 to 100 dB, roughly the equivalent of a jackhammer. These levels vastly exceed the World Health Organization’s recommended threshold of 30 dB to be able to rest. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. The monitor escalates to an urgent, repeating multi-tone musical sequence engineered to demand immediate human attention. Studies across international health systems reveal that clinical staff encounter hundreds of alarm signals per shift, up to 90 percent of which require no clinical intervention, for example because a patient mistakenly presses the buzzer when they move. headline_hi: समुद्री प्रवाल को मिली नई ज़िंदगी
summary_en: Scientists in the Florida Keys have conducted an experiment to save corals. In August 2024, divers placed floating shades over twenty colonies of brain coral. These shades were constructed using PVC frames and nylon mesh. They were suspended in the water about thirty centimeters above the coral. These shades were not cooling the water; instead, they were blocking intense sunlight and ultraviolet rays. The twenty corals kept beneath this protection began to regain their color. Meanwhile, the twenty unshaded corals turned pale and faded due to the heat. This study has been published in 'Frontiers in Marine Science'. Karen Neely, lead researcher from Nova Southeastern University, shared that they wanted to evaluate methods to protect corals for the future. She noted that measures like shading can offer short-term protection on a small scale.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: How a floating shade can help coral survive a marine heatwave
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM When divers installed floating shade structures over 20 colonies of brain coral in the lower Florida Keys in August 2024, the corals underneath began recovering their color. The 20 colonies left unprotected grew paler through the hottest stretch of the season. That was during 2024’s second-highest heat stress year on record at the site since 1985. The results appear in Frontiers in Marine Science . The shades were made from PVC frames and nylon mesh, suspended roughly 12 inches (30 centimeters) above the coral. They weren’t cooling the water. They were blocking the intense sunlight and ultraviolet radiation that amplifies heat-related bleaching. Why Florida’s 2023 heatwave made this study necessary In the summer of 2023, a record marine heatwave hit the Florida Keys. At most monitored sites, every kind of coral bleached. Branching corals, including the staghorn and elkhorn species, were nearly wiped out. At one inshore location, more than half of the corals researchers were tracking lost some or all their living tissue. Karen Neely of Nova Southeastern University, the study’s lead author, described the umbrella project as a direct response. “This study stemmed directly from that event: we wanted to provide proof of concept for tools to save targeted corals in similar future events,” she said. “ Heat-related coral bleaching is probably the biggest threat to reefs worldwide. Solutions like shading can offer temporary protection on small scales.” The scale of the global bleaching crisis Scale is where the Florida experiment runs into its limits. summary_en: A European energy developer has launched a large biomethane plant in southern Italy. This plant is located in Grottole, Italy. It will produce an alternative to natural gas from agricultural waste. This will save approximately nine thousand tonnes of carbon dioxide each year. The plant will generate forty-five gigawatt-hours of renewable energy annually. Through this new initiative, more than three thousand households will receive renewable gas.
